It does not mean that the configuration was exclusive to western China, because provinces belonging to the pathway may also be found in other regional groups.

The conditions defining S3b provide a possible interpretation of this regional difference. The configuration combines government data openness, informatization, and a high share of e-commerce enterprises with the absence of strong direct policy support. The higher mean coverage observed in western China suggests that some western provinces may have developed combinations of public-data access, digital processing capacity, and enterprise participation that support data application without intensive direct policy intervention. This interpretation concerns relative configuration coverage and does not imply that western China as a whole possesses stronger digital infrastructure or higher new quality productive forces than the eastern and central regions.

S3b therefore represents a cross-regional application-led pathway with comparatively stronger western representation. Its regional distribution also illustrates the heterogeneity within China’s broad geographical divisions: some western provinces may possess relatively developed open-data platforms, informatization capacity, and e-commerce activity even though the western region is often described as having weaker average digital and market foundations.

The descriptive results further show that the average coverage of the six configurations was generally higher in central and western China than in eastern China. One possible explanation is that recent digitalization and green-transformation initiatives in central and western regions have generated more concentrated development patterns. Provinces at similar stages of digital and industrial development may also be represented by the same configurations more consistently. These interpretations remain tentative, however, because the Kruskal–Wallis tests did not identify statistically significant regional differences for five of the six pathways.

The lower average coverage observed in eastern China should not be interpreted as evidence of weaker new quality productive forces. Eastern provinces generally possess more diversified industrial systems, more mature digital markets, and a wider range of development trajectories. This diversity may reduce the proportion of cases represented by any single configuration. In other words, lower configuration coverage may reflect greater pathway differentiation rather than inferior development performance. The eastern region may rely on more varied combinations of data infrastructure, enterprise capabilities, market institutions, and policy arrangements that are not fully represented by one dominant model.

Overall, no statistically significant regional difference was detected for five of the six configurations, whereas S3b showed a significant difference in province--level within-group coverage across the three regional groups. S3b was represented more strongly in western China, but it remained a cross-regional rather than an exclusively western pathway. The result reinforces the need for place-sensitive digital-governance and urban–regional development policies. Regions should not simply replicate a nationally uniform data-market model; policy design should reflect the particular combination of public-data access, digital capacity, enterprise participation, and institutional conditions already present in each location.

sec.title: 6.1. Research conclusions
sec.p: Drawing on transaction cost theory, resource orchestration theory, and institutional theory, this study examined how market-oriented data allocation was associated with regional new quality productive forces across 31 provincial-level regions in China from 2018 to 2023. Dynamic QCA was used to identify alternative sufficient pathways and to evaluate their temporal stability and regional variation. The analysis produced four main conclusions.

First, no individual antecedent condition constituted a necessary condition for high regional new quality productive forces. Although informatization and the marketization environment displayed comparatively high necessity consistency and coverage, neither reached the required consistency threshold of 0.90. Regional new quality productive forces therefore cannot be attributed to a single data exchange, policy intervention, technological condition, or institutional factor. They arise from the joint operation of several conditions whose roles vary across configurations.

Second, six sufficient configurations were identified. Their individual consistency values ranged from 0.907 to 0.980, while overall solution consistency and coverage reached 0.929 and 0.792, respectively. The configurations were classified into three broader models: the Scale–Environment Model, the Level–Scale–Environment Model, and the Level–Scale Model. The Scale–Environment Model was organized around e-commerce participation and the marketization environment. The Level–Scale–Environment Model combined informatization and market institutions with either government data openness or big data exchanges. The Level–Scale Model depended on enterprise participation together with data-exchange infrastructure or the combination of government data openness and informatization. These models demonstrate equifinality: regions with different digital, market, and institutional foundations can reach high levels of new quality productive forces through different pathways.

Third, the six configurations were generally stable over time. Their between-group consistency values remained between 0.85 and 1.00, and all between-group adjustment distances were below 0.20. The pathways nevertheless followed different temporal trajectories. The consistency of the Scale–Environment Model generally increased, whereas that of the Level–Scale Model gradually declined. The Level–Scale–Environment Model followed a V-shaped pattern. These movements indicate changes in the relative explanatory consistency of the pathways rather than the emergence or disappearance of the configurations. The results suggest that enterprise participation and general market institutions became more closely associated with the outcome over the study period, while pathways relying primarily on data access and application capacity displayed a weaker tendency in later years.

Fourth, no statistically significant regional difference was detected for S1a, S1b, S2a, S2b, or S3a. S3b was the only configuration for which province-level within-group coverage differed significantly among eastern, central, and western China. Its mean coverage was higher in western China, indicating that the pathway was more strongly represented among western provincial cases during the study period. S3b combined government data openness, informatization, and a high share of e-commerce enterprises with the absence of strong direct policy support. The result suggests that some western provinces developed an application-led pathway based on public-data access, digital capacity, and enterprise participation. However, S3b was not exclusive to western China, and the regional difference should not be interpreted as evidence that western regions had higher overall levels of new quality productive forces.

Overall, market-oriented data allocation contributes to regional new quality productive forces through combinations of transactional infrastructure, resource-application capacity, and institutional conditions. The results do not support a uniform development model. Effective policy requires alignment between existing regional capabilities and the conditions that are absent or underdeveloped. This configurational perspective is particularly relevant to urban and regional development because provincial data institutions shape the digital infrastructure, enterprise ecosystems, public-data access, and innovation resources available to the cities located within them.

sec.title: 6.2. Policy implications
sec.p: Develop differentiated systems for government data openness and institutional support. Government data openness should be treated as part of a wider institutional and technical system rather than as a stand-alone publication activity. Provincial and urban authorities should improve data standards, metadata quality, updating procedures, interoperability, access conditions, and mechanisms for lawful reuse. Central and western regions with less developed public-data systems should give priority to basic platform capacity and the usability of released datasets. Legal rules, intermediary services, transaction procedures, fair-competition mechanisms, and data-security responsibilities also require attention because access alone does not ensure productive application.

Eastern regions generally possess more mature digital infrastructure and open-data systems. Their policy focus can move toward public-data authorization, clearer allocation of data-related rights, cross-jurisdictional circulation, and the development of replicable governance practices. Cooperation among eastern, central, and western regions should not be limited to transferring technical platforms. It should also cover data standards, institutional experience, professional training, and mechanisms for connecting regional data resources with urban public services and industrial applications.

Use e-commerce ecosystems as practical settings for data application. The Scale–Environment Model shows that e-commerce participation and a favorable market environment can partly compensate for limitations in formal data exchanges or direct policy support. Central and western regions can build on locally distinctive industries to develop e-commerce clusters and digital supply chains. Agriculture, specialized manufacturing, cultural products, logistics, and regional services can provide concrete settings in which data are generated, circulated, and applied. Such ecosystems can support early-stage data marketization before formal data exchanges become fully developed.

This finding does not imply that e-commerce platforms can permanently replace data exchanges. Their functions differ. E-commerce ecosystems create application demand and commercial data flows, whereas exchanges provide standardized and compliant channels for formal data transactions. As regional data markets mature, the two should become more closely connected. Eastern regions can take a leading role in linking e-commerce platforms, data exchanges, and digital-industry clusters. Platform firms can gradually develop services related to data processing, transaction support, compliance management, and ecosystem coordination while participating in the design of transparent pricing and transaction arrangements.

Coordinate data infrastructure, informatization, and market institutions. The Level–Scale–Environment Model indicates that data exchanges and government data openness are most effective when they are supported by informatization and a functioning market environment. Investment in platforms alone is unlikely to produce lasting results when regions lack digital professionals, data-processing capacity, enterprise demand, or predictable institutional rules. Data-market policies should therefore be coordinated with broadband and computing infrastructure, digital-skills development, software and information-service industries, and support for enterprise-level applications.

Central and western regions should continue to address gaps in information infrastructure and digital human capital, but investment decisions should be linked to identifiable industrial and public-service needs. Government intervention is most useful when it establishes common standards, removes institutional barriers, and enables participation by firms and other organizations. It should not substitute for enterprise initiative or create platforms with limited transaction and application demand.

Eastern regions face a different challenge. Their diversified industrial systems and mature digital markets make reliance on a single pathway less appropriate. Policy should permit experimentation across data trading, public-data reuse, industrial digitalization, urban governance, and cross-regional data circulation. Greater attention should also be given to interoperability among existing platforms and to the institutional coordination needed to prevent fragmentation.

Adopt place-sensitive strategies for urban and regional development. Provincial data-market policies have direct consequences for cities because urban areas concentrate enterprises, infrastructure, public services, and data-intensive activities. Provincial authorities should allow cities with different industrial structures and digital capacities to follow different development pathways while maintaining common rules for data security, interoperability, and lawful circulation. Major metropolitan areas may focus on cross-sectoral data integration and advanced data services, whereas smaller cities may begin with public-data applications and the digital transformation of locally important industries.

The regional concentration of S3b also shows that western regions should not be treated as uniformly dependent on direct policy support. Where government data openness, informatization, and enterprise participation are already relatively strong, policy can focus on removing remaining transaction barriers and allowing existing market actors to expand data applications. Direct intervention should be calibrated to local conditions rather than applied with the same intensity across all regions.

sec.title: 6.3. Limitations and future research
sec.p: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the spatial unit of analysis was the provincial-level region. This scale allowed consistent comparison across China and captured broad institutional and economic differences, but it may conceal substantial variation among cities within the same province. Provincial capitals, metropolitan regions, resource-based cities, and smaller prefecture-level cities may differ considerably in digital infrastructure, government data openness, industrial composition, and enterprise capabilities. The results should therefore be interpreted as provincial configurational patterns rather than direct evidence of city-level mechanisms.

Future research could extend the analysis to prefecture-level cities or metropolitan regions. City-level data would make it possible to test whether the provincial pathways remain valid at a finer spatial scale and to identify the conditions under which provincial policies are translated into urban development outcomes. Multilevel designs could also examine how provincial institutions interact with city-level infrastructure, industrial specialization, and governance capacity.

Second, the analysis covered the period from 2018 to 2023. Although the panel structure made it possible to examine temporal stability, the six-year period was relatively short compared with the institutional development cycle of data-factor markets. The observation window did not capture the complete transition from the initial establishment of data exchanges and open-data platforms to the formation of mature transaction and application systems. Some of the pathways identified here may change as legal frameworks, digital infrastructure, and enterprise practices continue to develop.

Longer panel datasets should be used when additional annual observations become available. An extended observation period would allow future studies to distinguish short-term fluctuation from structural change, identify possible transitions between configurations, and assess whether the relative importance of market institutions, government data openness, and enterprise participation changes as data markets mature.

Third, government policy support was measured through the frequency of data-market-related terms in provincial government work reports. This measure captures the degree of policy attention but cannot fully distinguish among regulatory, financial, infrastructural, and organizational policy instruments. It also does not directly measure implementation quality, expenditure, enforcement, or actual policy outcomes. Regions with similar term frequencies may therefore differ considerably in the substance and effectiveness of their policies.

Future studies could apply more detailed policy-text coding to distinguish policy objectives, instruments, target groups, and implementation mechanisms. Text-based indicators could also be combined with policy expenditure, implementation records, regulatory documents, project completion data, or interviews with public officials and market participants. Such evidence would provide a more precise account of how different forms of government intervention interact with market and technological conditions.

Fourth, the temporal comparability of government data openness requires further attention. The Open Data Forest Index captures several relevant dimensions of provincial data openness, but the availability and construction of annual observations may not correspond perfectly to the complete 2018–2023 study period. Any inconsistency in annual coverage could reduce the precision of the dynamic comparison. Future research should use fully harmonized annual indicators or reconstruct comparable measures directly from provincial open-data platforms.

Finally, QCA identifies set-theoretic associations and alternative sufficient pathways, but it does not by itself establish the detailed causal processes through which each configuration produces the outcome. The regional cases discussed in this study illustrate the substantive meaning of the pathways but do not replace in-depth case evidence. Comparative case studies, interviews, process tracing, and mixed-method designs could be used to examine how data exchanges, public-data platforms, enterprises, and government institutions interact within particular regions. Combining these approaches with dynamic QCA would provide a fuller understanding of how market-oriented data allocation contributes to new quality productive forces and how these mechanisms influence urban and regional development.
